body: The other shoe cannot be found — twenty to eight on a Tuesday, and the middle one is still looking. There is a consent form for the trip that has to be signed and it is somewhere under the fruit bowl, and the eldest has remembered, at the door, with her coat on, that she needs a plain white T-shirt today. The toast is in the toaster and will be discovered there at four in the afternoon. Somebody says grace over nothing in particular, because the youngest is already sitting down and it seemed a shame to waste him. It lasts nine seconds. Then the door goes twice and the house is empty and the kettle has boiled itself cold.

Those nine seconds are the family devotional. Nobody planned them, nobody prepared anything, and they are the only part of that morning that will happen again tomorrow, in the same place, at the same point in the sequence.

The literature on raising children in the faith is almost entirely about content — what to teach, which verses, which questions to expect and at what age. Very little of it is about the actual obstacle, which is that there are four people, three schedules, one bathroom and eleven minutes.

Logistics is a military word long before it was an office one. It is the business of getting the right thing to the right place at the hour it is needed, and it is famously the least glamorous discipline in any army — nobody writes a ballad about fuel. It is also the one that decides outcomes. A force with better tactics and worse supply loses to a worse force that can feed itself. Households run on the same arithmetic. The question is never whether a parent wants their children to know God. It is whether the thing they have chosen to do about it can survive a Tuesday in November when two of them are ill.

The dial is one small piece of that supply line. 46 of the 121 frequencies are on air, running day and night, which is a dull technical fact that turns out to matter enormously: a thing that is always already playing costs a household nothing to start.

This is not the advice anybody wants to be given. Telling a tired parent that their problem is scheduling rather than devotion sounds like a snub, and telling them that the fix is a fixed point rather than a deeper prayer life sounds like a small answer to a large question. Nobody teaches this because it does not sound spiritual. It is, however, the part that decides whether any of the rest happens, and a decade of families quietly giving up in week three is a high price to pay for keeping the subject dignified.

The whole culture of it runs the other way. Family faith is sold as a project: a curriculum, a course, a plan with a first day and a wall chart. That framing feels serious and it carries a hidden defect, because anything with a start date implies an end date, and anything with a wall chart can be visibly failed. Miss four days and the chart is now evidence. Very few households abandon the faith. A great many abandon the scheme, quietly, some time in February, and then carry a low-grade sense of having been found out — which is a strange thing to have bought with something intended to help.

Look at an ordinary week and count what is genuinely fixed. Meals, mostly. The journey to school and back. Bedtime, which is non-negotiable because the alternative is a household that never sleeps. Sunday morning, if that is your habit. That is not very many points, and they are all already occupied by something else — which is exactly what makes them useful. A fixed point does not need to be defended, remembered or begun. It happens whether or not anybody is feeling devout that day.
What survives contact with a real week is whatever was attached to something that was already going to happen.

The designed family devotional deserves a fair hearing, because it is better in almost every respect. It teaches more. It is ordered, so the children get the whole shape rather than the parts their parents happen to like. It treats them as people worth preparing for, and children can tell when they have been prepared for. The trouble is not quality. The trouble is that it needs a slot of its own, and a slot of its own is the first thing a week takes back. It is cut in week three, and the parent files it privately as a spiritual failure rather than a scheduling one, and that misfiling does a great deal of damage over ten years.
The families who keep something going are almost never the most devout. They are the ones who bolted it to a fixed point.

A man who has not managed a family devotional in eleven years of trying stands on the landing every night at the moment he turns off the light. He says the same eight words at the door of the boys’ room. He did not choose them; they are the ones his own father used, and he has never been entirely sure he agrees with all of them. It takes no time at all and he has never once thought of it as teaching. His eldest is nineteen now and rang in March at an indefensible hour to say that he had had a bad week. His father could not think of anything to say, so he said the eight words down the phone, and the boy said them back.

Nothing in that required a plan, a curriculum or a good week. It required one sentence to have been attached to one moment that was going to happen anyway, for long enough that it stopped being a decision.

It has to be said that this is a small thing to build on, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. Nine seconds is nine seconds. A grace said out of habit can be said by somebody who does not mean a word of it. You will teach your children a routine and you will not know, for a very long time, whether you taught them anything else. A station playing under a kitchen is not catechesis and should not be sold as one.

But the smallness is not a compromise on the way to something better; it is the mechanism. What a household can carry when it is tired is the only thing it will still be carrying in ten years, and ten years is the unit that matters here. Nobody was ever formed by an intensive. People are formed by the thing that was there every single evening, unremarkable enough that nobody had to agree to it, until the shape of it was in them and they could not say when it had arrived.

So the honest method is unromantic and it is short. Do not design a family devotional. Find the thing that already happens every day without anybody deciding — the meal, the journey, the light going off on the landing — and put something true next to it. Then leave it there and stop assessing it. That is why a station that is simply on does more work in a house than a programme nobody can find the moment to start.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The band runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70, and the frequencies do different jobs. Most of it is music — praise and worship, gospel, country, hymns and a great deal besides. Some of it is teaching and prayer. Some of it is built for children, and safe to leave running in a room with them in it whether or not every track names God out loud. And 40 of the frequencies are international, hosted in 29 languages for the nations rather than translated into them afterwards, which matters in more kitchens than people assume — plenty of households pray in one language and argue about shoes in another.

For the case this article has been describing, start at HM 308.70 — Year of Jubilee. It is the flagship, it carries continuous worship and teaching from the Inspire Family catalogue, it runs day and night, and it will not play you the same song twice in a day. What recommends it here is not the catalogue but that it asks nothing of the person switching it on. There is no title to choose, no episode to resume, and no decision to be made at twenty to eight by somebody holding a consent form and one shoe. It is already playing. That is the entire feature, and it is the only feature a Tuesday morning has room for.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card — open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is already in the kitchen and press play. It is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have, and you can add the page to a home screen if you want it nearer. Do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies households are really reaching for at which hours — which is how the next station gets built.

So do not start a plan this week. Pick the fixed point you already have — the one that happens whether or not anybody is on form — and put one true thing beside it. Put HM 308.70 on when the kettle goes on, and then forget about it. In a month you will not be able to say when it became the sound of that hour, and in ten years one of your children will use eight words at a door somewhere else, and will not remember being taught them.
